children: By Anoop Menon
Dubai Electricity & Water Authority's (DEWA) international arm should aim to run three or four successful operations abroad within five years, a senior McKinsey partner said.
Success should be measured by projects operating in different markets, not agreements signed, according to Amadeo Di Lodovico.
"Global champions don't grow linearly; they grow exponentially," he said during a panel discussion at World Green Economy Summit (WGES) in Dubai.
He added that DEWA International could outgrow its parent within two decades.

Di Lodovico cited high operational standards, a single system integrating power and water, and long experience with private developers. The Dubai brand, reinforced by DP World and Emirates, adds weight abroad.

The utility ranks first globally in 13 key utility performance indicators and two regional benchmarks across generation, transmission, distribution and customer service, according to an official statement issued in June 2026.

Arshad Mansoor, chief executive of the Electric Power Research Institute, said DEWA's real export is a technology vision for every project. "It's not one technology but a combination: batteries, drones for inspection, and being one of the first utilities to adopt AI," he said.

He also listed DEWA’s focus on grid-enhancing technologies, underground transmission and recycling of renewable assets, and said seven phases of the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park taught DEWA how to future-proof projects.
“DEWA looks at the specification of future weather before building today,” he said.

Danny Touma of PwC Middle East said DEWA's range, from thermal to renewables and batteries, could help DEWA International partner with developers at a time when AI is driving demand for round-the-clock power.
The opportunities

PwC estimates $151.1 trillion of capital will be needed for infrastructure through 2050, $36 trillion of it for power, Touma said. McKinsey sees $17 trillion through 2040, about a third in power and water, according to Di Lodovico.
Both pointed to the convergence of power, water, cooling and AI data centres. Touma said three data centre offtakers terminated contracts in the past month because power arrived too slowly.

“Building a data center costs around $40 million per megawatt (MW), compared with a power station, which might be a million dollars per MW,” he said. “If you have the capability to either wrap a solution or deliver power and water at speed in a complicated environment, it can really differentiate you.”
He indicated there are opportunities beyond Europe's established FLAP-D hubs — Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris and Dublin.
“A lot of the AI infrastructure was built in the FLAP-D markets, but if you're looking at big training models, you don't necessarily have to be there,” he said.

Mansoor suggested Saudi Arabia and Qatar as natural early markets, and the US as harder but potentially lucrative over five to 10 years. He said about 80 percent of the top gas turbine makers' next five years of output is heading to North America.

Touma urged acquiring not just assets but developers and platforms, forming joint ventures within those platforms to gain local experience and create hubs for expansion into other European markets, the US and Africa.
Valerio Capizzi, Global Lead Utilities, ING Bank said Europe has realized that energy security cannot come from renewables and nuclear.

“Growing concerns over security of supply have reinforced the need for a diversified energy mix, which includes gas and hydropower, alongside opportunities to repower and upgrade existing generation assets,” he said.
“There is a significant need for additional capex to upgrade, applying AI and other innovation to create the right balance with renewables,” he said.

However, he cautioned that underinvestment, bureaucratic hurdles, local opposition and supply chain shortages have hampered efforts to upgrade Europe's ageing power grids, leaving many investors unable to secure grid connections to deliver renewable electricity.
The challenges
Di Lodovico cautioned that DEWA's success rests partly on Dubai's unusual utility-state relationship. "But the foundations for a successful story [for DEWA International] are clearly there," he said.
Mansoor said DEWA's reliability record partly reflects a compact grid fed by a few large high-voltage lines. "You don't design your own grid in other countries; you get what you get," he said.
He also warned that local opposition to infrastructure projects, which DEWA hasn't faced at home, will likely follow DEWA International abroad.

Di Lodovico underlined that the key differentiator when expanding internationally is not capital alone, but the value a company brings through technology, project execution or operational efficiencies. He advocated a phased approach, allowing the company to test strategies, learn from experience and adapt to local market conditions.

Touma cautioned against replicating the Gulf's risk allocation model in overseas markets and urged early wins to demonstrate capability and credibility. He recommended building a geographically diversified portfolio across developed, emerging and Gulf-adjacent markets to balance risk-adjusted returns with expertise and capabilities.
The panellists agreed that choosing the right partners would be critical to DEWA International's success overseas.
“Pick the right partners, have cultural alignment, be true to what you’ve promised, and hold your partner to it too,” advised Touma.

Di Lodovico recommended two types of partnerships: local partners who understand market dynamics, have established relationships and bring different risk perspectives; and government-to-government partnerships, given the heavily regulated nature of utilities and the broader socioeconomic considerations surrounding infrastructure development.
Mansoor summed up the importance of collaboration with an adage: “If you want to walk fast, walk alone. If you want to walk far, walk together.”

Capizzi pointed out that the influx of capital in the industrial sector seeking quick returns is at odds with the long-term nature of the utilities business, where assets can remain operational for decades.
“It’s an industrial business and needs long-term investment and long-term vision rather than a quick win, because with a quick win we can’t go that far,” he said.
(Reporting by Anoop Menon; Editing by SA Kader)
